WCBIP 2026 · WIIP Session · Melbourne · 5 December 2026

From Challenges to Change

Women Advancing Interventional Pulmonology in Resource-Limited Settings
Dr Lamya CHRIF MORAND
Interventional Pulmonology Unit
International Hospital Kenitra
Ibn Tofail University, Kenitra, Morocco
lamya.chrif1@uit.ac.ma
Disclosure: no relevant financial relationship.
[0:55] Good morning, colleagues and friends. It is a privilege to join this session alongside women who have helped shape interventional pulmonology. Today I want to take you beyond individual career stories, and ask a broader question: what does it take for a talented woman to become an interventional pulmonologist when the training, technology, and institutional support are not readily available? This is not a talk about women as victims of circumstance. It is about women as builders of opportunity, and about the systems we must change so that excellence is not determined by geography. ---- TO CONFIRM: the disclosure line "no relevant financial relationship" and the wording WCBIP 2026 requires (same line as the sister talk). The central question

Talent Is Everywhere. Opportunity Is Not.

One finds a route
  • A fellowship
  • A simulation center
  • Protected training time
  • Mentors
Same motivation, same talent.
The other builds one
  • Finds a trainer abroad
  • Pays for the travel
  • Negotiates time away from work
  • Returns to a unit without the equipment
What happens when the gender gap meets the resource gap?
2
[1:05] Consider two equally motivated young pulmonologists. Both want to learn advanced bronchoscopy. One has access to a fellowship, simulation center, protected training time, and mentors. The other must find a trainer abroad, pay for travel, negotiate time away from work, and return to a unit without the necessary equipment. If the second physician is also a woman navigating unequal expectations or limited sponsorship, the barriers may compound. We must not assume that every woman experiences the same barriers, but we should investigate and address the structures that make opportunity unequal. ---- No open item. The two physicians are an illustration, not data.
Evidence · global health

A Leadership Gap Persists

67.2%
of the global health workforce are women (2024 update)
Participation alone does not guarantee the power to decide.

67.2%: WHO, National Health Workforce Accounts, 2024 data.

World Health Organization. Closing the leadership gap: gender equity and leadership in the global health and care workforce. Policy action paper. Geneva: WHO; 2021. ISBN 978-92-4-002590-5

~25%
of senior leadership roles held by women (WHO estimate, 2021 data)
3
[1:10] The first layer of evidence comes from global health. According to the WHO, women account for 67.2 percent of the global health workforce in the 2024 update. Yet an earlier WHO policy analysis estimated that women occupied only around a quarter of senior roles. These estimates refer to different years and populations, so they should not be interpreted as a single contemporaneous ratio. But they illustrate a consistent pattern: participation alone does not guarantee decision-making power. This matters in procedural specialties because leaders influence who gets training, protected time, funding, and access to equipment. Evidence: WHO, Closing the Leadership Gap (2021; 2024 workforce update) ---- Fact check 2026-11-14: OK. 67.2%: WHO National Health Workforce Accounts, 2024 data (web page of the report); 25%: estimate based on data available in 2021 (report, Key messages, printed p.2). 4
[1:20] Now look specifically at interventional pulmonology. Brock and colleagues surveyed 92 physicians in 17 countries. Among respondents, 23 percent of women versus 60 percent of men held leadership positions, a statistically significant difference. More than one in four women reported gender discrimination, compared with around one in twenty men. This was a small, nonrepresentative survey; it does not tell us the global prevalence of discrimination or establish causality. But it makes the problem visible within our own specialty. Our response must go beyond encouragement and include access to leadership pathways. Evidence: Brock J et al. Respiration. 2023;102:613–620. doi:10.1159/000531581 ---- No open item (fact check 2026-11-14: OK. Leadership 23% of women vs 60% of men, p = 0.002; discrimination 26.8% vs 5.3%, p = 0.023). Worldwide IP training survey

A Second Divide: Access to Training

70%

41%

Respondent reports from a convenience sample, not country level prevalence estimates.
5

Chrif Morand L, Corbetta L. Respiration. 2026. doi:10.1159/000552099

[1:20] Our worldwide survey examined 102 responses across 34 countries. Seventy percent reported that their country lacked a structured IP training program. Forty-one percent described no exposure to interventional techniques in general pulmonary training, while 96 percent supported a standardized global curriculum. These are respondent reports from a convenience sample, not country-level prevalence estimates. Nevertheless, the contrast is striking: we are rapidly advancing robotic bronchoscopy and other technologies, while many colleagues still lack a predictable route to basic procedural competence. Equity begins with education. Evidence: Chrif Morand L, Corbetta L. Respiration. 2026. doi:10.1159/000552099 · n=102, 34 countries ---- No open item (fact check 2026-11-14: OK). A single international fellowship cannot be our only solution.
7
[1:25] Our first pan-African survey gives us a closer view. Fifty-one interventional pulmonologists from sixteen countries participated. Forty-nine percent reported no structured training. Among those who had received structured training, 84.6 percent trained outside Africa. Only 24 percent reported radial EBUS availability. These data describe participating clinicians, not the whole continent, and they do not provide sex-stratified estimates. They are still valuable because they identify practical constraints: local training pathways, equipment, and geographic access. They show why a single international fellowship cannot be our only solution. Evidence: Chrif Morand L et al. An analytical framework, not a measured effect

The Double Barrier

At the intersection: fewer routes to autonomy and leadership

Conceptual synthesis: intersectional effect not quantified in cited IP surveys.

8
Gender barriers
Resource barriers
Double barrier
Gender related
  • Recognition
  • Sponsorship
  • Access to leadership
  • Unequal care responsibilities
Resource related
  • Limited equipment
  • Few training centers
  • High costs
  • Low procedural volume
[1:15] Here is the conceptual heart of this talk. On one side are gender-related barriers: recognition, sponsorship, access to leadership, and unequal care responsibilities. On the other are resource-related barriers: limited equipment, few training centers, high costs, and low procedural volume. Their intersection may make advancement harder, but we need to be precise: our existing surveys have not directly measured the interaction between gender and resource scarcity. Rather than claiming a number we do not have, let us use this framework to design the next generation of research—and the next generation of solutions. Evidence: Conceptual synthesis; intersectional effect not quantified in cited IP surveys ---- No open item. The kicker keeps the framework from reading as a measured effect. Moved from the slide (voice note 2026-11-14): "Not measured in our surveys: a framework for the next research."
The patient pathway

What Scarcity Means in Practice

Pan-African IP survey 2026: pathways illustrative, not causal estimates.

9
01
Late referral
delayed diagnostic bronchoscopy
02
Travel to sample
no local advanced sampling, referral abroad
03
Limited tissue
fewer diagnostic options
04
Unequal access
patients, trainees and services
For the patient
Referred late, sent far for sampling, or facing a system without the technology.
For the young physician
No proficiency in a procedure her unit cannot perform.
[1:15] Resource constraints are not abstract. They affect patients and professionals together. A patient with a suspicious pulmonary lesion may be referred late, travel to a distant center for advanced sampling, or face a system without consistent access to the relevant technology. At the same time, a young physician cannot become proficient in a procedure that her unit cannot perform. This is why the development of women in IP is not simply a workforce question. It is connected to service delivery, diagnostic equity, and the future of thoracic care. We should be careful not to claim that these surveys prove specific delays or outcomes; they identify capacity gaps that warrant measurement. Evidence: Pan-African IP Survey 2026; pathways illustrative, not causal estimates ---- No open item. The four stations are illustrative: do not quote delays. Systematic review · 91 studies

Mentorship Helps, but Is Not Enough

Shen MR, et al. Acad Med. 2022;97(3):444-58. doi:10.1097/ACM.0000000000004563

  • Mentoring is associated with career success.
  • Women were more likely to have no mentor.
Who opens the doors
A mentor
offers guidance
A sponsor
helps open doors
An institution
makes those doors possible to walk through
Mentoring must be structured, accessible and tied to sponsorship.
10
[1:15] Mentorship is a powerful lever, but we must define what it can and cannot do. A systematic review of 91 studies in academic medicine found associations between mentorship and career success, while women were more likely to report having no mentor. These studies are not specific to interventional pulmonology or low-resource settings, and association does not establish that mentoring alone causes promotion. The practical implication is clear: mentoring must be structured, accessible, and connected to sponsorship. A mentor offers guidance. A sponsor helps open doors. An institution makes those doors possible to walk through. Evidence: Shen MR et al. Acad Med. 2022;97:444–458. doi:10.1097/ACM.0000000000004563 ---- No open item. WIIP as a platform for action

From Individual Mentoring to Networks

  • Cross border mentorship for isolated colleagues
  • Peer networks that make expertise visible
  • Research and speaking opportunities
  • New leaders who create opportunities locally
Measure outcomes
A new skill?
A paper?
A service?
A new mentor?

WIIP initiatives: program examples; outcome evaluation needed. Visual: Rise to Lead mentorship program, WiIP Strong.

11
[1:10] This is where international communities such as WIIP can contribute. Cross-border mentorship connects colleagues who might otherwise remain isolated. Peer networks make expertise visible. Research collaborations and speaking opportunities build academic and professional credibility. But I want to move the conversation from participation numbers to meaningful outcomes. Did a mentee gain a new skill? Publish a paper? Establish a service? Become a mentor herself? These are the outcomes we should measure. A network becomes transformative when it develops new leaders who then create opportunities locally. A practical competency model

Training Should Be a Pathway, Not an Event

Training survey: Chrif Morand L, Corbetta L. Respiration. 2026.

12
01
Accessible theory

02
Simulation
before supervised patient procedures

Gerretsen ECF, et al. Chest. 2023;164(4):952-62. doi:10.1016/j.chest.2023.05.012

Workshop with manikin and Constantina, photo to come
11 of 14
studies: simulation improved most measured outcomes
Transfer to patient performance: limited evidence.
[1:25] The next step is to build training pathways, not simply organize isolated workshops. I propose four connected components: accessible theory, simulation, supervised clinical practice with a logbook, and objective assessment. A 2023 CHEST systematic review found that eleven of fourteen studies reported positive effects of bronchoscopy simulation on most measured outcomes. However, evidence of transfer to actual patient performance remains limited. So simulation is necessary as a preparation tool, but it cannot replace supervised clinical competence. For women in resource-limited settings, structured pathways can reduce dependence on informal networks and unpredictable opportunities. Evidence: Chrif Morand & Corbetta 2026; bronchoscopy simulation review, CHEST 2023 ---- TO ADD (voice note 2026-11-14): the photo of a training workshop with a manikin and Constantina, which Lamya will send; it replaces the framed slot (244 x 140, camera mark and small caption, kept on purpose until the photo arrives; review 2026-11-14). The hub and network model

Build Locally. Connect Globally.

Regional hubsimulation, supervised cases, assessment
Nearby hospitalslinked to the hub, regional faculty
Global partnersmentorship and quality assurance
Women design, lead, teach and evaluate.

Proposed implementation framework: not an evaluated intervention.

Regional hub
Nearby hospitals
Global partners
13
[1:15] A sustainable model needs local ownership. Imagine a regional hub that can deliver simulation, supervised cases, and assessment. It is linked to nearby hospitals, supported by regional faculty, and connected internationally for mentorship and quality assurance. This is more sustainable than relying exclusively on travel abroad. International collaboration should not create dependency; it should build local capacity. And women should not simply be invited to attend these programs. They should help design them, lead them, teach in them, and evaluate their impact. Evidence: Proposed implementation framework; not an evaluated intervention ---- No open item. The diagram is a proposal, not an evaluated model (source line).
A research and accountability agenda

What Should We Measure by 2030?

Disaggregated by gender, region and resource context.
Access
Who can access training: slots, travel support, equipment
Equity
Who completes it: selection, retention and leadership by gender
Competence
Who achieves independently assessed competence, with case logs
Patient impact
Referral to diagnosis time and diagnostic yield
Without measurement, good intentions remain invisible.

Proposed indicators: not validated targets; no 2030 targets claimed.

14
[1:15] If we want this movement to be scientific, we need indicators. Let us measure who can access training, who completes it, who achieves independently assessed competence, and who moves into leadership. Data should be disaggregated by gender, region, and resource context. And crucially, we should connect workforce development to patient-facing measures such as referral-to-diagnosis time and diagnostic yield. These are proposed indicators, not validated targets. Without measurement, good intentions can remain invisible. With measurement, we can learn what actually works and where investment has the greatest impact. Evidence: Proposed indicators; no 2030 targets claimed ---- No open item.
The action agenda

Five Commitments for Our Community

None requires perfect circumstances. Each requires collaboration and leadership.
01
Invest in access to training
not just attendance at meetings
02
Create regional programs
competency based
03

guidance, and doors that open
04

as faculty, program directors and decision makers
05
Publish the data
equity metrics, training outcomes, patient outcomes

Action agenda: informed by WHO, IP surveys and mentorship literature.

15
[1:05] So I would like to end with five commitments. First, invest in access to training, not just attendance at meetings. Second, create regional competency-based programs. Third, combine mentorship with sponsorship. Fourth, make women visible as faculty, program directors, and decision-makers. Fifth, publish the data: equity metrics, training outcomes, and patient outcomes. None of these requires us to wait for perfect circumstances. Each requires collaboration, leadership, and a willingness to redesign systems that were never equally accessible to everyone. Evidence: Action agenda informed by WHO, IP surveys and mentorship literature ---- No open item.
Closing message

The Future Is Built by the Doors We Open

Talent is everywhere.
Opportunity must be, too.
From isolated success stories to systems of opportunity.
The women who come next

Photo: women in IP, AABIP 2025.

16
[0:55] I began with a simple statement: talent is everywhere, opportunity is not. I want to end by challenging us to change that. The measure of progress is not only how many women reach the top of interventional pulmonology. It is how many new pathways we create for the women who come next, and how many patients benefit because those pathways exist. Let us move from isolated success stories to systems of opportunity.
